title: Length-scale interactions in ductile fracture of multiphase materials under bending
abstract: Abstract Ductile fracture under bending is governed by interactions among length scales associated with the imposed deformation field, material microstructure, and defects. Here, we use dual-phase advanced high-strength steels as a model system to examine these interactions through large-scale, microstructure-based finite element calculations. The dual-phase microstructure is modeled explicitly in the near-surface region of bend specimens. The ferrite/martensite feature size and specimen thickness are systematically varied to examine structural–microstructural length-scale interactions. Non-metallic inclusions are introduced to examine defect–microstructural length-scale interactions. The results show that microstructural refinement delays strain localization and crack nucleation, improving bendability for a fixed structural length scale. However, the extent of improvement depends on sheet thickness. The calculations further show that inclusions become especially detrimental when their size exceeds the microstructural length scale. Thus, bendability is governed not by a single material or geometric length scale, but by the coupled effects of specimen geometry, microstructure, and defect length scales. The findings have implications for designing high-strength multiphase sheet materials, where microstructural refinement is often pursued to increase strength and enable thickness reduction.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials Theory

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Ductile fracture, which occurs through the nucleation, growth, and coalescence of microscale voids, is the dominant fracture mode of metallic materials at room temperature (Benzerga et al.  1 ). In a homogeneous deformation field, these processes depend on the material microstructure and the presence of defects, if any. However, in heterogeneous deformation fields, such as those imposed by bending, the local stress and strain states vary over a structural length scale that can be much larger than the microstructural features (Zheng et al.  23 ; Liu et al.  9 ; Zheng et al.  22 ). This raises a fundamental question: how do structural, microstructural, and defect length scales interact to govern ductile fracture?

Bending-induced ductile fracture of multiphase sheet metals provides a simple yet meaningful setting to examine this question (Liu et al.  9 ). It imposes a well-defined structural length scale through the specimen thickness while simultaneously producing a highly heterogeneous deformation field. The tensile side of the bend specimen is most susceptible to void nucleation and crack initiation, but the local fracture process depends on the details of the underlying microstructural features of the multiphase material in this region. If additional defects such as inclusions are present, their influence is also expected to depend not only on their absolute size, but also on their size relative to the surrounding microstructural features (Liu et al.  10 ).

Bending is also technologically important because many sheet metal forming and manufacturing operations involve bending-dominated deformation paths, and bendability often limits the use of high-strength sheet materials (Sriram et al.  15 ). Dual-phase advanced high-strength steels provide an ideal model material system for studying this problem (Tasan et al.  18 ; Liu et al.  10 ). Their ferrite/martensite microstructure introduces a well-defined microstructural length scale, their ductile fracture mechanisms under tensile loading conditions are well documented, and they often contain a small population of non-metallic inclusions that provide additional defect length scales (Liu et al.  10 ).

As a prominent class of advanced high-strength steels, dual-phase steels combine high strength, ductility, and energy absorption through a carefully engineered multiphase microstructure (Rashid  12 ; Kuziak et al.  8 ; Bhattacharya  2 ; Tasan et al.  18 ). Their microstructure consists primarily of hard martensite particles dispersed in a relatively soft and contiguous ferrite matrix (Rashid  12 ; Tasan et al.  18 ). The ferrite phase provides ductility, while the martensite phase promotes high early-stage strain hardening and high ultimate tensile strength (Davies  4 ; Srivastava et al.  16 ; Zheng et al.  23 ), making these steels attractive for automotive crash-resistant components.

In this work, we use dual-phase advanced high-strength steels as a model system to examine how geometry, microstructure, and defects jointly influence ductile fracture under bending and limit bendability. The present work builds on our previous microstructure-based bending studies. In Liu et al. ( 9 ), we developed a methodology for microstructure-based modeling of ductile fracture under bending in dual-phase materials and examined how bending-induced heterogeneous deformation interacts with the underlying heterogeneous microstructure to govern crack nucleation and early-stage crack growth. Extending this framework, Liu et al. ( 10 ) examined the influence of non-metallic inclusions, including their size, location, and nucleation strength, on bendability. In contrast, the present work treats the structural, microstructural, and defect length scales themselves as independent variables. The objective here is therefore not simply to examine whether microstructure or inclusions affect bending fracture, but to demonstrate how multiple coupled length scales govern ductile fracture under bending. To this end, we carry out large-scale, microstructure-based ductile fracture calculations in which these length scales are systematically varied.

The  Results and discussion  section is organized to demonstrate how these length scales interact. We first examine self-similar scaling and then consider the independent and coupled effects of sheet thickness, ferrite/martensite feature size, and inclusion size. The calculations show that, for a fixed structural length scale, refining the microstructural feature size improves bendability, consistent with prior experimental observations that refined or more homogeneous microstructures can improve ductility and bendability (Shi et al.  14 ; Suppan et al.  17 ; Samei et al.  13 ). However, this improvement is not universal; its magnitude depends on the structural length scale imposed by the bending configuration. In addition, the effect of inclusions is controlled by their size relative to the surrounding microstructural features. These findings are important because microstructural refinement is often pursued to increase strength and enable the use of thinner sheets (Kuziak et al.  8 ; Bhattacharya  2 ; Joost  7 ). Thus, under bending, the benefit of refinement must be evaluated together with the accompanying structural and defect length scales.

sections.heading: Problem formulation and numerical method
paragraphs: The material model and numerical implementation are the same as in Liu et al. ( 9 ,  10 ). Here, for completeness, we briefly describe the formulation and the procedure used to vary the structural, microstructural, and defect length scales.

For calculations involving defects, a single circular non-metallic inclusion is introduced in the microstructure-resolved region. The inclusion is located on the tensile side and at the center of the bend specimen along the length direction. The inclusion size is varied to examine the interaction between the defect length scale and the microstructural length scale. In these calculations, the inclusion is modeled using the stress-controlled nucleation relation described below.

The use of a thin slice with overall plane strain boundary conditions is a computational idealization that allows the microstructure to be resolved while keeping the calculations tractable. This approximation is most appropriate for representing the central region of a wide bend specimen away from free edges, which is expected to be well approximated by plane strain. However, it does not capture three-dimensional stress variations along the bend axis or out-of-plane variations in microstructure and inclusion morphology. Such out-of-plane variations may influence the precise crack nucleation site and the three-dimensional crack growth path. Therefore, the present calculations should be interpreted as isolating the role of in-plane structural, microstructural, and defect length-scale interactions, rather than as complete three-dimensional predictions of crack morphology.

The use of different nucleation criteria reflects the different physical mechanisms represented by the matrix phases and the inclusion. In the ferrite and martensite phases, void nucleation is taken to be strain controlled because damage in the dual-phase microstructure is associated with plastic deformation and progressive nucleation at microstructural heterogeneities such as ferrite/martensite interfaces (Zheng et al.  23 ). In contrast, non-metallic inclusions are treated as brittle particles or weak particle/matrix interfaces for which void nucleation is promoted by tensile normal stresses and hydrostatic tension, consistent with bend-failure observations in advanced high-strength steels (Fan et al.  5 ; Sriram et al.  15 ). The stress-controlled nucleation relation is therefore used to represent inclusion cracking or inclusion/matrix decohesion driven by the local tensile stress state.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: The calculations are organized to isolate the effects of structural, microstructural, and defect length scales on ductile fracture under bending. We begin by considering the effect of the structural length scale by varying the sheet thickness while keeping the characteristic ferrite/martensite feature size fixed. We then examine the effect of the microstructural length scale by varying the characteristic martensite feature size at fixed sheet thickness. The interaction between these two length scales is then analyzed by varying both quantities. Finally, the effect of a single non-metallic inclusion is considered to examine the interaction between defect and microstructural length scales.

Note that the constitutive framework described in  Problem formulation and numerical method  section is local and does not include strain-gradient plasticity or any other intrinsic plasticity length scale. Thus, the length-scale effects discussed herein arise from interactions among the imposed bending field, the resolved microstructure, and inclusions, rather than from size-dependent changes in the ferrite or martensite flow strengths.

sections.heading: Effect of structural length scale
paragraphs: However, the subsequent crack growth path differs between the thicker and thinner specimens. In the thinner specimen, the crack grows along a dominant band of intense plastic strain localization and reaches the half-thickness of the sheet. In the thicker specimen, the crack path is more tortuous and meanders before reaching the half-thickness of the specimen. Thus, changing the structural length scale alters the ductile crack growth path and, consequently, the macroscopic flexural strain to failure shown in Fig.  2 b.

sections.heading: Effect of microstructural length scale
Interaction between structural and microstructural length scales
paragraphs: The strength of each dependence, however, is controlled by the other length scale. The effect of microstructural refinement is stronger for thicker specimens and becomes weaker as the sheet thickness decreases. Similarly, for finer microstructures, changes in the structural length scale have a more pronounced effect on bendability, whereas for coarser microstructures, the dependence of bendability on sheet thickness is relatively weaker. This clearly shows that structural and microstructural length scales do not contribute independently to ductile fracture under bending. Rather, the beneficial effect of microstructural refinement is amplified when the structural length scale is large enough for the bending-induced strain gradient to interact strongly with the microstructure. Conversely, when the sheet thickness is reduced, the gain in bendability associated with microstructural refinement is diminished.

sections.heading: Interaction between microstructural and defect length scales
Concluding remarks
paragraphs: In this work, we carried out large-scale, microstructure-based finite element calculations to understand length-scale interactions in ductile fracture under bending. Dual-phase advanced high-strength steels were used as a model material system. The structural length scale associated with the bending geometry, the microstructural length scale associated with ferrite/martensite phase morphology, and the defect length scale associated with non-metallic inclusions were varied to examine their effects on crack nucleation, early crack growth, and bendability.

The results show that, in the absence of any size effect on the elastic-plastic response of the material, bendability is governed by relative length scales rather than by a pure scaling of the problem. Thus, when the structural and microstructural length scales are scaled together, the macroscopic flexural response remains essentially unchanged. However, when these length scales are varied independently, both the flexural strain to failure and the crack growth path change. Increasing sheet thickness improves bendability for a fixed microstructural length scale, while microstructural refinement improves bendability for a fixed sheet thickness.

The improvement from microstructural refinement is associated with changes in strain localization near the tensile surface. Finer microstructures promote several relatively narrow localization bands, whereas coarser microstructures promote fewer but wider bands of intense localization. These wider bands promote earlier nucleation and coalescence of sub-surface micro-cracks. Importantly, the benefit of microstructural refinement is not independent of sheet thickness; it is stronger for thicker specimens and becomes weaker as sheet thickness decreases.

The consideration of an inclusion shows that the defect length scale must be considered relative to the surrounding microstructural length scale. Small inclusions have little effect, but inclusions become increasingly detrimental when their size becomes comparable to or larger than the characteristic microstructural feature size. Since ferrite/martensite feature size and inclusion size are controlled by different processing routes, reducing the microstructural length scale does not necessarily reduce the defect length scale.

Overall, the results show that ductile fracture under bending is governed by coupled structural, microstructural, and defect length scales. For high-strength multiphase sheet materials, this means that the benefit of microstructural refinement must be evaluated together with sheet thickness and inclusion size.
